transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2026-11-05 15:00 PST | Duration: 57m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Avery Collins, Diego Martinez, Priya Nair, Sam Liu (Redwood) | Maria Chen, Raj Patel, Jasmine Lee, Omar Ruiz (Catalyst)

Summary:
- Purpose: scope POC pilot to decide between hosted, dedicated, or private deployment modes. Align on success criteria, workload sizing, benchmark plan, and timeline.
- Outcome: agree to run a 2-week benchmark with Redwood-hosted and dedicated runs; security docs to be exchanged; pricing and TCO to be provided.

Topics: success criteria, SLOs, throughput and concurrency, token profile, benchmarks (latency/throughput/cost), timeline, security requirements (SOC2/KMS/VPC).

Action items (see metadata list above).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery Collins: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh Maria Raj thanks for making time. quick yes?
[00:06] Maria Chen: yeah thanks, excited. we want to make sure the pilot actually answers our main question which is: can we serve recommendation summarization at sub-300ms p50 and keep cost under our target of $0.0009 per token on average.
[00:20] Raj Patel: and to add our traffic shape is spiky — we see short bursts during campaigns, peak concurrency maybe 180 to 220 concurrent requests — so we need to understand burst capacity and degradation behavior.
[00:34] Diego Martinez: okay that's helpful, that gives us a starting point. quick clarifying q: what's the typical token distribution — input vs output?
[00:40] Jasmine Lee: roughly 250 input tokens average, output around 120 tokens. tail 99th token counts pushes to ~2k for long queries but rare.
[00:52] Priya Nair: got it. so for the pilot we'll want to test two working points: steady-state (50–100 qps) and peak burst (200 qps) with both average and tail token sizes.
[01:05] Omar Ruiz: security note — we need SOC two, ISO 27001, SSO/SAML, and KMS integration. if we go private we need air-gapped options cause of PII constraints for some stores.
[01:18] Avery Collins: yes we can share our compliance pack; for KMS the private and dedicated routes support customer-managed keys; hosted supports BYOK via our KMS integration but we'll send the specifics.
[01:30] Maria Chen: can you explain tradeoffs quickly between hosted and dedicated from a latency and cost per token perspective?
[01:37] Diego Martinez: sure. hosted is fastest to start — no infra lead time — but on high sustained throughput dedicated usually wins on unit cost because you can reserve GPU pools. latency on hosted is generally very good p50~150ms for smaller models, for larger LLMs p95 is more variable depending on noisy neighbors and region. dedicated gives you predictable p95 and you can tune quantization and batching policies. private gives the most control but add ops overhead and license negotiation for on-prem.
[02:05] Raj Patel: noisy neighbor concern is real — if we need strict p95 under 500ms can't risk shared tenancy spikes during campaigns.
[02:12] Diego Martinez: understood. we do two things to mitigate: smart routing and automatic fallback to smaller model variants if the primary can't meet SLOs; and reserved burst capacity on dedicated which is what Redwood Dedicated offers.
[02:25] Maria Chen: talk me through the benchmark itself — what will you run and what data you need from us?
[02:30] Diego Martinez: we'll need a 72-hour baseline trace of production traffic ideally, or a representative synthetic histogram if you can't share traces. payloads, average token length, concurrency pattern, and any special tokens or embeddings. we'll run A/B runs: 3-day hosted run, 3-day dedicated run with same workload replay, and a throughput microbenchmark to characterize max QPS per instance type.
[02:50] Priya Nair: for the microbenchmark we usually do step ramp up until 95th latency hits target or we saturate GPU. we'll capture p50/p90/p95 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and cost per million tokens.
[03:05] Jasmine Lee: what instance types are we expecting? our infra prefers A100 equivalents in prod.
[03:10] Diego Martinez: we'll recommend A100 and an 80GB variant for larger model runs; for smaller models a T4/RTX type sim might be possible for cost sims. we'll provide kernel and quantization profiles — if you want, we can run INT8 quantized runs to show cost/latency tradeoffs.
[03:26] Maria Chen: does Redwood do KV caching of recent requests? we have a lot of repeated context for customer history.
[03:30] Priya Nair: yes — automatic prefix caching and KV cache reduces token generation work for repeated contexts. note cache hit rate will depend on your request distribution; we'll measure effective token savings in the benchmark.
[03:44] Raj Patel: ok timeline? we'd like pilot results before black friday-ish, so end of November would be ideal.
[03:50] Avery Collins: realistic timeline: security docs and pricing this week, benchmark kickoff in ~10 days, 2-week run finishing ~2026-11-30. that fits your timeline.
[04:00] Omar Ruiz: about private deployment — can you outline what's involved? our legal requires data residency in EU for some clients.
[04:06] Diego Martinez: private deployment options: VPC-hosted private control plane (Redwood manages control plane, data path in your VPC) — faster than on-prem; or full on-prem package with air-gapped installers if required. both support HSM/KMS integration and audited logs. dedicated reserved capacity falls between hosted and private on ops overhead.
[04:26] Maria Chen: cost ballpark for dedicated? we need to compare to hosted TCO for our expected tokens.
[04:31] Avery Collins: we'll send a side-by-side TCO spreadsheet. rough rule: if sustained throughput exceeds X (we calculate from your concurrency and token size) dedicated tends to reduce per-token cost by ~20–40% depending on commitment term and model quantization. hosted has lower up-front but higher variable cost.
[04:49] Raj Patel: can we get an SLA on latency for dedicated?
[04:52] Priya Nair: dedicated customers can get SLA-backed latency windows at contract. we'll map p50/p95 targets in the pilot and if you sign reserved capacity we can attach more strict SLAs.
[05:02] Jasmine Lee: about instrumentation — what observability will be available during the benchmark?
[05:06] Diego Martinez: full Redwood Console access for the benchmark: per-route latency histograms, token-level cost breakdowns, tracing hooks, and raw logs export. we'll enable dashboarding for your SREs.
[05:18] Maria Chen: any gotchas with model versions and rollouts? we want deterministic behavior across runs.
[05:23] Priya Nair: we'll pin model versions and provide a deterministic seed where applicable. for private/dedicated we can snapshot configs; for hosted we'll use pinned variants and immutable container images for the run window.
[05:34] Omar Ruiz: security follow-up — audit logs retention, role-based access controls, SSO. do you support fine-grained RBAC?
[05:40] Avery Collins: yes we support SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC. audit log retention tiers are configurable — we'll share default retention and longer-term options.
[05:48] Raj Patel: competitor question — we've seen claims from SageCloud about lower latency using proprietary kernels. how does Redwood compare?
[05:55] Diego Martinez: we benchmark kernel selection and compilation for different archs; in many cases we match or exceed latency claims because our runtime selects optimized kernels based on sequence length and hardware. we'll include comparative benchmarks where publicly available, though direct apples-to-apples sometimes depends on model and token profile.
[06:12] Priya Nair: one more note on cost: caching and batching policies can reduce tokens generated by up to 30% in our experience for repetitive contexts, so that helps both hosted and dedicated.
[06:24] Maria Chen: ok let's lock decision criteria — success if p50 < 300ms, p95 < 650ms, cost per token < $0.0010, and sustained 24h availability with graceful degradation under bursts. does that sound right?
[06:39] Avery Collins: that's a good starting SLO set. we'll run to those targets and report.
[06:45] Raj Patel: how will you surface fallback behavior in the console? we want to know when fallbacks occur and why.
[06:50] Diego Martinez: we'll log fallback events with reason codes (capacity, latency breach, model error) and surface them in the rollout dashboard.
[06:58] Jasmine Lee: for the benchmark we'll need a secure temporary creds exchange. what's the method?
[07:03] Priya Nair: we'll use short-lived tokens via our sandbox account and you can restrict IPs — if private you'll provide service account keys and we'll coordinate through your security team.
[07:15] Maria Chen: ok anything else on timelines or dependencies?
[07:18] Avery Collins: just to recap next steps — we'll send pricing and security pack; Diego will send benchmark plan and required artifacts; customer provides traces and sample payloads; schedule kickoff for 2026-11-16.
[07:30] Raj Patel: sounds good. thanks all.
[07:34] Avery Collins: great, we'll follow up in email and Slack. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: some technical terms may be slightly off (e.g., K V cache transcribed as K-V cache), speakers sometimes overlapped.
